newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac asks review of ethics laws after sheep clone.
newsitem.headline: Chirac asks review of ethics laws after sheep clone.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac asked France's ethics panel on Friday to review laws to try to ensure that a British breakthrough in cloning an adult sheep would not lead to human clones.

In a letter to the head of the National Consultative Committee on Ethics, Chirac said that 1994 French laws banned experiments on human embryos and conception of embryos for research, but did not explicitly mention cloning.

"I ask you...to fully analyse our regulations and to propose to me, if needed, the adaptations that may seem necessary to you to avoid any risk that these cloning techniques be used on man," Chirac wrote to ethics head Jean-Pierre Changeux.

Chirac said French laws were due for review only in 1999 but the cloning of the sheep by Scottish scientists announced last weekend, was "a technical advance recognised as decisive by the scientific community".
"It seems necessary to me to ensure that the legislation of our country is completely adapted to the new applications which have opened up," Chirac wrote.
Earlier in the week, U.S. President Bill Clinton ordered an urgent inquiry into the ethics of cloning.
On Monday France's Farm Minister Philippe Vasseur raised the spectre of six-legged chickens or six-legged sheep and promised stiff new controls if there were "monstrous" experiments with nature.
